cards.title: Billions of tiny steps
cards.body:
Every tap, every video frame and every game move comes down to the **CPU** following instructions. Each one is tiny, like "add these two numbers" or "copy this to there".

The trick is speed: a CPU gets through **billions** of these steps every second.

cards.title: The clock
cards.body:
A [[CPU]] works to a beat, like a drummer keeping time. Each beat is a **tick** of its **clock**, and the CPU moves its work forward on every tick.

Clock speed is measured in **gigahertz (GHz)**. One gigahertz means **one billion ticks per second**, so a 3 GHz CPU ticks three billion times a second.

To keep the maths simple, this course counts **one step per tick**. Real CPUs can manage several steps in a tick, or need a few ticks for a hard step.

cards.prompt: A [[CPU]] runs at **2 [[GHz]]** and does one step per tick. A job takes **10 billion** steps. How many seconds does it take?
cards.hint: 2 GHz means 2 billion steps every second.
cards.explanation: 2 GHz is 2 billion steps a second, so 10 billion steps take 10 ÷ 2 = **5 seconds**.
cards.nudge: Think of GHz as billions of steps each second. How many seconds of those steps add up to the whole job?

cards.title: More cooks in the kitchen
cards.body:
Most CPUs today have several **cores**. Each core is a complete worker that can follow its own instructions, like having several cooks in one kitchen.

Some jobs split nicely: four cooks can chop a big pile of vegetables four times as fast. Others can't: a cake takes just as long to bake however many cooks are watching it.

So more cores only help when the job can be **split into pieces that don't wait for each other**.

cards.prompt: Saving your finished video (called **exporting** it) takes too long. Add **cores** until it finishes in **3 seconds or less**.
cards.explanation: A video is made of separate frames, so the work splits evenly. One core takes 12 seconds, two take 6, and **four** take 3.
cards.hint: This job splits evenly, so each extra core takes a share. Watch the timer as you add cores.
cards.nudge: Keep adding cores and watch the timer. The job has to finish in 3 seconds or less.

cards.prompt: Can extra cores share the job, or must it go **one step at a time**?

items.label: Treasure hunt: each clue finds the next
Knitting a scarf, row by row
A board game played one turn at a time

cards.explanation: Photos, files and frames are separate pieces, so each core can take some. A treasure hunt, a scarf knitted row by row and a turn-by-turn game all **need the answer to the step before**, so extra cores just wait.
cards.hint: For each job, ask: does every piece need the answer from the piece before it?
cards.nudge: Separate pieces can be shared out between cores. If each step needs the step before, extra cores just wait.

cards.prompt: Working hard makes the CPU hot. Tap the **CPU** and the part that **cools it down**.
cards.explanation: The **fan** sits right beside the **CPU** and blows the heat out through vents in the case. If the vents are blocked, the heat stays in, and a CPU that gets too hot **slows itself down** to stay safe. This is called **throttling**. Most phones have no fan: they spread the heat through the body, and throttle too.
cards.hint: You need two parts. The CPU is the square chip with a shiny lid. What have you met that moves hot air?
cards.nudge: Tap both parts: the CPU, and the part that blows hot air out through the vents so the CPU doesn't overheat.

cards.prompt: This laptop is on a blanket, working as hard as it can, and it's slowing down. Get it back to its full **3 [[GHz]]** without lowering the **load** (how hard it's working).
cards.explanation: When a CPU gets too hot, it **slows itself down** to stay safe. This is called **throttling**. The blanket blocked the vents and the fan was off. With both fixed, the heat can escape and the CPU runs at full speed.
cards.hint: Keep the load at full. What's stopping the heat from escaping, and what could move it away?
cards.nudge: Lowering the load isn't allowed here. A hot [[CPU]] slows itself down, so look for everything that traps heat or could blow it out.

cards.prompt: Laptop A has **4 cores** at 3 [[GHz]]. Laptop B has **8 cores** at 3 GHz. Which saves one big file faster, if the job **can't be split**?

options.nudge: Fewer cores doesn't make the one core doing this job any quicker. Compare how fast each laptop's cores tick.

options.text: Laptop B, because it has twice the cores
options.nudge: Extra cores only help when a job can be split into pieces. This one can't, so how many cores actually work on it?

cards.explanation: A job that can't be split runs on **one core**, whichever laptop it's on. Both cores tick at 3 GHz, so they finish together. Laptop B's extra cores only help with jobs that split.
cards.hint: Think of the cooks: can extra cooks help with a job that can't be split? Then compare the clock speeds.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The **CPU** follows billions of tiny instructions every second.
- **Clock speed** in **GHz** is billions of ticks per second.
- **Cores** are separate workers. They only speed up jobs that can be split.
- A CPU that gets too hot **throttles** (slows down). The fan and clear vents keep it cool.

That's the [[hardware]]. Next module: the software that runs the show.
